description:
NVIDIA's RTX 3070 Ti does little to help the current situation, especially considering that's silicon that could be pushed lower down the stack. Tested vs. RTX 3070, 3080, RX 6800, etc.
Sponsor: Get 10% off Squarespace purchases (https://geni.us/BqEpf)

You can find our review of the 3080 Ti that you shouldn’t buy here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vtkk-_0jrPU 
And our tear-down of the 3080 Ti here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UHo-fc6GG40

Our review of NVIDIA's RTX 3070 Ti Founders Edition video card looks at performance vs. the RTX 3080 Ti, RTX 3080, RTX 3070, and other cards, like AMD's competing RX 6800, RX 6800 XT, and even lower-down stuff like a 2060 or 1080 Ti. The RTX 3070 Ti benchmarks end up showing that the 3070 Ti is, at best, stagnation, or at worst, a decay in value proposition from the existing 3070 silicon. Unfortunately, NVIDIA has decided to push more expensive cards down the stack because of the current market conditions. This isn't as egregious as the 3080 Ti, sure, but perhaps that's the plan: The 3080 Ti makes this look almost sane by comparison, whereas the 3080 Ti is certifiably insane at $1200.

comments.text:
I think a 1080 performs relatively similar to a 3050 with frames and a 1080 ti compares with a 3060.  So if you were just looking to get the same kind of performance you're getting now on the games you're playing now, you could look into one of those.  Of course those cards may or may not scale the way your 1080 has over the years with new games you might want to play in the future. So whether you want to purchase some overhead is your call. 

The advantages you'll get from the RTX series will most meaningfully come from the ability to take advantage of DLSS.  If you're not familiar with that, do a quick search on it for full details.  But basically it allows you to play games at higher frame rates and resolutions than the card would normally be able to hand with it turned off at the cost of small image quality loss that's usually only noticeable if you're specifically looking for it.  

And in that sense, DLSS might actually give you similar scaling over time with a 3050/3060 as you got from your 1080. Because even if game start becoming more demanding on your gpu, you'll probably be able to use DLSS to scale with it.  Where as the 1080 can't use the DLSS feature in games.  So once games outgrow the 1080s capabilities, you'll definitely need to upgrade.  Where as you might still be able to make the 3050/3060 work with DLSS.  

RTX also gives you the ability to turn ray tracing on in games that have it.  Based on your comment, I'd imagine you'll find that feature trivial to meaningless.  But it is technically an advantage of the RTX line over the GTX cards.

comments.text: I think Linus had a valid point when we are talking about used hardware. I mean, obviously, product tiers still exist in the 2ndhand market and that's what the MSRP is based on. So, to some extent, the MSRP will still influence the 2ndhand prices. But on top of that, since it is a 2ndhand market, what the community is willing to pay for it, basically supply and demand, will also partly influence the 2ndhand prices. So, there are 2 factors generating the overall 2ndhand prices, and the consumer valuation of the product, in the case of GPU obviously rely a lot on performance. BUT when we are talking about scalped prices or resale prices of new hardware here, then yes it would be strongly correlated with the MSRP it launches with since it is a NEW product. I think you (Steve) and Linus are making points on two different prices.

comments.text: The second hand is sellers which have no standing business relationship with the manufacturers or their downstream distribution network. Which means the manufacturers have no control over the pricing of the products by these entities. Additionally as agents in these markets do not have any particular PR & optics to manage (at least on an individual level) pricing becomes directly tied to what the market will bare in a strict supply & demand sense. Thus the prices are more tightly coupled to performance of the product. This means if the msrp is too high the cards will just not be bought by scalper s for sale on the secondary market full stop the scalpers will not raise their prices because of the higher msrp they will just exit the market.

comments.text:
I crunched the numbers, and calculated relative price performance of the cards controlled for performance (based on gpu.userbenchmark.com).

When adjusting for the performance difference, the price/performance at msrp seems to have no significant effect on the price/performance of the resale value. Except for 6800/XT, all of the more expensive cards have roughly 90% of the value of the cheaper comparison card (in price/performance), with the range going from 83% to 95%.

By comparison, the value based on msrp ranges from 60% (2060 vs 2080) to 112% (980 vs 980ti). These correspond to a resale value differences of 88% and 94%. Also, since the 980ti came 3 quarters after the 980, while the 2080 came out 2 quarters BEFORE the 2060, there is a relative age difference of up to more than a year that adds to relative value of the 980ti/980 value (as compared to the 2080/2060 value).

The 6800XT seems to be a few % better value than the the 6800, both based on MSRP (107%) and resale (103%). I think this could be simply a case of UserBenchmark having an inflated performance difference. It reports that it has 120% of the perormance, but other sources put the difference closer to 10%. Using that figure, or simply by removing this outlier, virtually all correlation between msrp value and resale value vanishes.

1 point to Linus for this one.

TLDR: Dont buy gpus atm, but if you do the TIs are probably not stupid.

Here in Sweden you can buy a new 3080 for roughly  $2.2k or a scalped one for $1.8 Comparing that to the (Swedish)MSRP of $0.8k this means that prices for 3080 are 225% of MSRP. For a 3080 Ti you can buy it in store for $2.1k compared to the (swedish)MSRP of $1.3k thus the price is 161% MSRP, but this is for a Suprim X card that never would have sold for MSRP considering that the real price is closer to 130% of MSRP.

The 3080TI price hike should've been to 1100 with the extra 2gb of GDDR6X and slight increase in performance. It is no secret that the 3080FE left almost no room for margin for Nvidia with its expensive cooler, components and memory. Also frames are not the only area to equate value with except for gamers. Maybe budget editors need the extra couple gb of vram but can't afford a 3090 so they opt for the 3080TI. 

Truly I do think they were mainly trying to increase margins but relative to what they made on the first run I don't think it is evil of them. They are after all a business.

I think they could've waited one more generation for GDDR6X and that would've made them great margins while still being able to produce good value with barely, if any performance loss for most people.

comments.text: I like data as much as anybody, but the data GN shows doesn't necessarily say what Steven thinks it does.  It simply shows a correlation between MSRP and street price.  Linus asserted that street price was determined by value to the customer and MSRP doesn't really effect it.  Steve's data would seem to refute that except that MSRP isn't random.  It's perfectly reasonable to assume that the correlation occurs because manufacturers have some UNDERSTANDING of the products value to the customer.  Essentially MSRP isn't driving street price.  A third variable, perceived value by the customer, is independently driving both MSRP and street price.  This is classic correlation does not equal causation error.  We should expect that manufactures have an idea of how valuable their customers will find a product and set MSRP accordingly just as we expect that street prices will also reflect how valuable the product is to customers.  The difference being because scalpers are trying maximize instantaneous profits PER UNIT, and manufacturers maximizing total profit across the entire product line and into the future (including ephemeral concepts like customer good will etc.) Put more simply a scalper with 100 GPUs needs to find the highest price that still sells all 100 GPUs.  A manufacturer who can keep making more GPUs needs to find a price that maximizes total profit over time, which might mean selling a ton of cards at a slim margin or just a few at a huge margin. The fact that these two prices are different and correlated is entirely expected and doesn't prove Linus wrong.

comments.text: I don't get why you would criticize 'second hand.'  It detracts from your other, valid points.  If I buy a card and re-sell it on eBay, that is a second hand purchase for the buyer, correct?  Also I don't think Linus was talking about MSRP setting the price floor on the second (or whatever you want to call it) hand market.  I think he meant the price of the item will be based on the performance of the card, not what the MSRP was of the card at launch.  If the 3080ti performed, say, 50 percent better for mining than the 3090 due to some software lock on the 3090 that doesn't exist on the 3080 and someone doesn't care to try to hack the lock (in my unrealistic example lol), the price of the 3080ti would be higher than the 3090 because it would be more valuable to the people who are currently willing to pay very high prices for graphics cards - namely those who will use the cards as a money making tool.  If I forecast that I will make $3,000 on a 3080ti in six months time, why would I not spend $2,000 on the card.  I mean, that is just money in the bank, and I probably would even be willing to pay more for the card.  A gamer, on the other hand, begins losing money immediately on such a purchase since the gamer isn't using the card as a money-making tool (unless he or she 'gets out' in the next 18 months or so and can sell the card for the same premium at which he or she bought it). So I think Linus' points are pretty valid, although you yourself have very valid points as well (I agree with your comparing the 3080ti to the 3080 on a tech channel since a gamer is much more likely to buy a 3080 at MSRP than a 3090 at MSRP).

comments.text:
I like both channels... it's possible folks... Steve is comparing apples to apples (MSRP to MSRP or Scalped to Scalped)... that makes sense of course... but what Linus is/has been saying is a real-world scenario... if you've literally been searching for MONTHS to buy ANY card at MSRP, and you can't get your hands on one and can't find one, but on launch day, there's a 3070Ti sitting on the shelf at MSRP... is it a great value compared to the 3070-non-ti at MSRP... no, it's not... but if your choice is "I can buy this 3070Ti NOW for $600, or I can buy a 3070 on E-Bay NOW for $1300... which is the better value?  That's a real-world scenario... Steve is living in that perfect world of comparing MSRP to MSRP or Scalped to Scalped... but as Steve himself said, this is a very special situation in the market we're going through... sometimes your ONLY choice is an MSRP card sitting on the shelf vs a scalped card on E-bay... is it a fair comparison?  No... but believe it or not... life isn't fair.

Bottom line... I agree with Linus's opinion... AND I agree with Steve's opinion.  They're both right... and they're both wrong.  I'll stay subbed to both channels.

P.S. I own a 3060... pretty much the last card of the 30-series I was interested in... and agreeing with Steve's review... it's not a great value... the 3060Ti or 3070 is a better value... but IN THIS MARKET, getting a 3060 at MSRP ($389) vs getting a scalped card or NO card at MSRP were the only choices I could get at the time.  The reality is, you take what you can get at MSRP if you can actually find one for MSRP... I'd been trying to get a 30-series card for MSRP since the 3070 launch last year and didn't get my 3060 till May... the 3060 was literally the ONLY card I was able to find at MSRP over all other cards... and it was a better value at MSRP than buying a scalped card off E-bay... sometimes comparing an MSRP vs Scalped is a real-world scenario.  Life isn't fair.

comments.text:
Not sure this proves your point against Linus though, you missed the final step in your rebuttal.

Your graph showed generally that MSRP and resale value are positively correlated, i.e. higher MSRP = higher resale value. This is basically going to be a given - nvidia/AMD will always price their cards in order of performance. The MSRP of the 3070Ti was never going to be higher than that of the 3080 for instance, so you would never have negative correlation to resale values (this counters one of your other points - nvidia does know that the 3070Ti will sell for way more than $600, but it still can't increase the MSRP over that of the 3080's $700)

Linus wasn't disagreeing with this. He was saying if relative performance and relative MSRP don't match, then resale value will follow performance instead of MSRP.
I've plotted your relative MSRP and relative resale value numbers against each other, and done the same with relative performance (https://www.tomshardware.com/reviews/gpu-hierarchy,4388.html) vs. relative resale values here: https://i.imgur.com/VjZFjO8.png

As it shows, relative performance is a better predictor of relative resale value. Think the 2080 vs. 2060 data point is unfair? Here's a graph that excludes it which still shows performance as a better indicator of resale value: https://i.imgur.com/bXsOivZ.png

You guys should be able to do a better plot using the actual resale/MSRP/performance numbers, since you've got your own data and not plotting a whole lot of relative data points.

comments.text:
So, now that I'm past that initial passive aggressive tirade that was the first half of the video I'ld like to make a few points.
First, just calling out his use of the general term "secondhand market" - which literally (check Merriam Webster) means buying something used but in a more broad/modern sense can mean buying something from a source that isn't an established retailer - with the multi-hand joke was excessively literalist-nitpicky even for me. I'll think it, but I'm not dumb enough to try to make even a half-joke about it.
Second, is that MSRP/Resale A/B graph. Just what are you trying to prove here? 2080 launch MSRP was $699, and so was the 3080. 2080Ti's launch MSRP was $1,199, and so was the 3080Ti. The only difference was the RTX Titan launching at $2,499, and the 3090 at $1,499. Scalper prices for the 3080 right now having just checked eBay's sold listings for them range from about $1,800 to $2,100 with an average delta of about +$1,200 or +171%. Scalper prices for the 3080Ti on eBay's sold listings range from about $2,100 to $2,800 with most around $2,400(high est.) giving it an average delta of about +$1,200 or +100%. Delta from $1,900 for the 3080 to $2,400 for the 3080Ti is 26%. Is the 3080Ti's performance difference vs the 3080 worth a 26% increase in cost? Nope. Because a major point Linus made that you skipped outright is that a buyer with that much money on-hand will typically not care. If they have the money now, they will buy the best they can get now. He went into a story - and I can validate this from my own experiences in electronics retail - about how if someone goes into a store ready to spend $4,000 on a PC, he would try to sell them on getting a $2,000 PC and save the other $2,000 for another 2 years later. Cost to performance, that makes sense. Most customers in that position do not care. They will spend the money they have. It's the consumer-conditioning we've all been exposed to, and most of us succumb to.
Lastly, you missed or didn't address the point about VRAM shortage. Likely the biggest reason for the existence of the 3080Ti in its current state is to get rid of 3090 silicon overflow in dealing with a GDDR6X shortage. There's rumor floating around that the 3090 has silently been discontinued because of it, or at least halted until VRAM supply can meet its demand. Does that justify its price? Yes. What doesn't justify its price is the 3080 being so close in performance. Just like supercars, designer clothing, and everything else that's more expensive than it's worth; people who have the money to buy it do not care. Meanwhile the savvy shoppers that are your and Linus's subscribers can see the price and the performance differences. They can make intelligent choices with their money, real or imagined. What they can't do it seems is read where Linus's video clearly stated they did not have an MSRP when they shot the video. For filling that performance gap between the 3080 and 3090, it does its job well. At a reasonable price? BEEP no! The 6800XT still wrecks face.

comments.text:
I have an issue with this chart. Raw performance and MSRP is only one factor. 5 out of the 8 examples shown here also have different VRAM capacities. That can very possibly explain the disparity between the street prices. The 980 only has 4GB, which by today's standard is pretty paltry. So I can understand why the 980ti would command a much higher price, it not only offers better performance, but it is FAR less likely to become bottlenecked by VRAM. Your own testing has fully demonstrated this. This also extends to the GOAT 1080ti. It not only offers more performance than a 1080, but also 3 more GB of VRAM. The 1080ti basically never gets bottlenecked by VRAM capacity, and that is...kind of important. The 1080ti is also well reknown, it was the king for such a long time, and frankly its reputation is likely a large factor as well. There is simply something about owning a flagship product, even a slightly older one, that appeals to some people. That can translate to a higher street price. This might sound like a silly thing, but I think the data is showing this. It may also explain the Vega 64 and 56 comparison.
You can see this sort of thing with any product, where the label on the product increases value simply because of the name on the tag. I think it is safe to assume that even the great PC Master Race is susceptible to this concept.

Not every single buyer of GPUs is looking at straight performance. You also have a variety of people who may use their GPU for other tasks like Blender, but cannot afford a Quadro or Titan. The 1080ti remains very popular with this crowd in part because of its VRAM, and you can bet the 2080ti can also holds its value for a similar reason. The 1070 has always been a popular card, being one of the cheapest cards to offer a 8GB buffer. So again, it makes a lot of sense why the 1070 would command such a strong price over the 1060 6GB.

I think it is worth noting that 3 cards that all have the same VRAM capacities happened to all show the lowest increases over all on this chart. So while they are close to a 1 to 1, the increases are still pretty low in comparison.

I find it very odd there is not a single x80 versus x70 on this chart. This would be logical, IMO, since most x70 and x80 class cards offer the same VRAM capacities. Plus these are not flagships, and thus do not carry the same aura about them that a x80ti will.

bruh i'm gonna have to agree with Linus' take on this one, which is: the second-hand market will more clearly determine the actual (or real-world) value of a GPU, which is ultimately decided by customers, not manufacturers, AND--the performance-to-price comparison of ALL the available GPUs on the market, and not just this generation's lineup (which considers BOTH MSRP and second hand prices). In my opinion, Steve's take is quite theoretical or abstract, whereas Linus' take is more practical or real-world. So you can say "well Nvidia said it should be this price for this GPU, and now it says the follow-up GPU that's only 5-10% better in performance is 80% higher in price, which means muh corpration is tryna rob us gamers!"... but that doesn't say anything useful to a real-world market of GPU shoppers. 

with some hindsight, it kinda seems like for the performance offered, Nvidia undersold their 3000 series launch, because look at what people were comparing it to: the $1200 2080 ti! so compare the 2080 ti performance and MSRP to the 3080 performance and MSRP. that's quite a gap ($500) for comparable peformance! it left quite a bit of room (even "invited") resellers to scalp. furthermore, you could say that the value proposition for the 3000 series was so insanely good, that like a pressure cooker it made the secondhand market explode through the roof! and so, i believe the 3000 Ti-series launch is more of a market corrective (or price corrective in relation to the market), to help contribute to a normalizing of prices. the corrective won't be felt immediately, but it will otherwise speed up a return to normal pricing, imo.

so, all that is to say: i'm wondering, why you all mad? for all the data Steve colleceted, were there a few pieces he forgot to consider? ultimately, it's the market/consumers that finally determines prices/value, not the producers/manufacturers.

and now, for some conspiratorial speculation: it seems almost like the techtubers who negatively reviewed the 3080 ti because of price are tryna use their audiences as leverage against "muh big corporation", as if they can persuade Nvidia (and others) to lower their prices....hmm... and btw, i haven't heard anyone talk about the 3000 ti-series MSRP in relation to rising inflation the last few months...

I'm honestly kind of surprised that Linus wouldn't think that the scalping wouldn't correlate with price considering how long he was an inventory manager. After working at Micro Center and Best Buy for years and dealing with scalpers, usually these people ARE NOT tech people. They just find out that X item can be bought and sold for a profit, so they do that. I've had people who have bought Graphics Cards, Consoles, Processors, Motherboards, and even ram a couple a years ago without any intention of using it. They don't know the performance numbers, they just know what they bought it for and that they can get roughly x amount or x% more than what they paid. It doesn't matter what it is, just as long as a profit can be made. For example with the PS5 and Xbox launches scalpers were obviously buying the consoles, but they were also buying absurd amounts of peripherals because again, they knew they could sell them for more (this didn't last nearly as long thankfully). 

Yes, the used market does usually work the way that Linus says (*intel i7 processors do not follow this trend in the time I've spent building PCs for clients), but this isn't the used market. It's the new market, and in a time where components are basically a mirage its a really bad new market.

comments.text: In fairness, Linus was talking about the 3080 Ti. Steve saw it as the expensive version of 3080; Linus saw it as the reasonable version of 3090 (cheaper, easier to cool, easier to build in volume amidst chip shortage (including VRAM shortage)). Each is right in his own way, but considering that the performance of the 3080Ti is almost exactly that of the 3090, I'm leaning towards Linus. It's just that the 3090 pricing, even at MSRP, is so insane (a 2.15x price increase for no more than 1.2x the performance) that you definitely pay a heavy premium for the extra performance over the 3080, even with the new card. But for the people contemplating the 3090 (and those cards are selling in whatever number they can be produced), the 3080 Ti is a downright reasonable proposal. Ergo, like I said, I'm closer to Linus on this one.

comments.text:
I think they're valid points on both sides,

On one hand the idea that MSRP does not effect aftermarket pricing and it's purely based on performance is a bit nuts. For example a 3080 street price in the UK currently is around £1600. The 3090 street price is not £1800 as Linus would have you believe if you go by performance based pricing, it's actually going for £2400. Even factoring in VRAM I'd say it's clear that MSRP is affecting the price. This means the cards are marked up by £950 and £1000 respectively, relative to the MSRP.

On the other hand the 3070 Ti isn't that bad, you're getting the same price to performance across the 3070, 3070 Ti and 3080. I actually calculated it earlier based on MSRP and performance per dollar does not vary that much until you hit the 6900xt, 3080 Ti and 3090. You could (in theory) pick your price point under this and go with it without making any actual mistake as far as $/FPS goes. 

I do agree with Linus though that the 3080 Ti has a place and comparing it to the price/performance of the 3080 is pointless, the cards for those who want the best of the best as far as gaming performance and it offers it at $300 less than the 3090. It's still a bad choice for gaming, it's just less bad and less wasteful than a 24GB 3090.

I also like to look at GPU price to performance with regards to the final net cost, rather than in a vaccum since GPUs are not standalone products. For example let's assume your setup (computer minus GPU, desk, chair, mouse, keyboard etc)  costs $800. You can then decide between a $300 GPU and a $700 GPU. You're actually deciding between paying a net cost of $1100 or a net cost of $1500.  Since the GPU is going to dictate your gaming performance for the most part, the $1500 system will likely double the performance of the $1100 system, so you're paying $400 more on a $1100 purchase to double the performance. This is why I believe the 3080 is the best price to performance GPU for most people or at least it would be if you could actually buy it.

Anyway, this has been my Ted Talk on why lower price GPUs are usually not particularly good as far as price to performance goes, while offering another way to look at it. Judging the most important component for gaming in a vaccum does not make for an accurate overall cost analysis in terms of relative performance.

I want to say I do think it’s a little weird how fixated reviewers get on percentage differences in price and performance. The value of money differs between people and even for the same person, it’s not necessarily linear, and likewise for performance.

The thing that I don't understand about linus's argument here is that MSRP scales with performance as well. Companies don't release a more powerful card for cheaper than a less powerful card within the same generation. The used market ebbs and flows based on something's performance but so did the MSRP to begin with so what's his argument? It doesn't really make much sense.
MSRP will always have an effect on everything from scalping to used. Scalpers starting prices are usually a multiplier of MSRP and move around from there. 

In normal times MSRP directly effects used sales unquestionably. Older used cards are priced roughly where they would sit performance wise vs. the current gen product and it's MSRP. So, for example, the 2080 is basically just a 1080ti with RT cores. So, a used 1080ti would never regularly sell for more than what a 2080 would have new because no one would buy it otherwise, they could just get a 2080 new for the same price. MSRP provides a soft cap on what someone can reasonably sell a used 1080ti for in that instance. 

Honestly? Linus's whole wan show rant was someone filibustering. It starts in bad faith when he takes a common turn of phrase as if Steve meant it literally and it devolves into word salad with a pinch of poor shaming. comments.text:
So I'm a scalper, I've sold 4 dozen GPUs in the last 3 months and have over $50,000 in revenue and I am constantly monitoring the fluctuations in prices. I also talk to other scalpers and I am a part of a few scalping groups. 

What I will say about GN's interpretation is that it can be applied to certain AIB partner cards that are AMD based. What us scalpers are seeing is that many AIB partners are pricing their AMD cards very close to what their performance level gets you if you were to buy a scalped card. This makes buying those cards for scalping not very feasible because of platform fees on places like eBay and Facebook Marketplace. You have to have a good amount of local face-to-face sales to make scalping those cards profitable. This also applies to a few 3090 and 3080 Ti models (I'm looking at you, Zotac AMP HOLOs) This makes it much easier to get one of those cards from an online retailer instead of a scalper. So high MSRPs definitely affects what people are actually paying, since even those high MSRP cards sell out very quickly. But it is a slightly different context than what the debate has turned into.

My take on the pricing in the scalped market is that it is primarily based off of how much the market is willing to pay for the highest performing card, which is the 3090. What people are willing to pay for a 3090 is what dictates what people are willing to pay for a 3080, 3070, 6900 XT, etc. This also applies to previous generation cards.. the performance of a 2080 Ti compared to the 3070 and 3080 absolutely dictates it's price in the 3rd party market. All of the previous generation cards are currently selling at prices compared to the latest generation's performance. We also see this phenomenon with EVGA's B-Stock and Zotac's refurbished cards that they both sell 1st party on their website. They are able to charge the highest MSRP that those refurbished cards were sold at when they were new because people are snatching them up as a "great deal" because a used 2080 Super still has a ton of performance. In normal market conditions those refurbished cards would NOT be selling for full New MSRP. I have bought many of these 1st party refurbished cards and so this isn't 2nd hand knowledge.

Also, what we've seen when a new card comes on the market, is that higher performing cards get a price increase in 3rd party sales, and lower performing cards have a slight decrease in price but do not experience as much change as the higher performing cards.

To give an overview of the scalping market, what we scalpers do is provide a scatter plot of prices and the buyers decide what they're willing to pay. Some buyers just want the lowest Buy it Now price and don't care about the specific card, just the specific GPU and sometimes not even then as they just want the best GPU for what their budget allows, and those buyers set the floor for pricing. Anything under this price gets bought by people with ebay search alerts because they want a video card at a lower price than what they can immediately buy it for. It is the buyers who don't wait for a particular price and just want a GPU right now that fits their budget that really dictate the price of all cards. Other buyers want a specific GPU (Color, factory overclock, pre-installed waterblock, etc.) And buy the lowest price of that even if it is hundreds of dollars more than the lowest priced version of that GPU core. Others want a specific GPU but want to wait until someone posts it for the lowest price that GPU core sells for and so they have ebay alerts and buy as soon as what they want is at a price they want. 

But again we come back to the people who are ready to buy right now and they will buy the best performance that their budget allows for. If their budget is $1,000 for a video card, they are going to buy a 3060 or 6700 XT because that's the highest performance that they can click a Buy it Now button on. And these people represent the majority of buyers. And those buyers come from different situations. Maybe their old video card died. Maybe they are finally done waiting for reasonable prices and just want to game right now. Maybe they are a business that has a customer who needs a new computer. Whoever they are, they are in my stated category of people wanting the best performance for Buy it Now and they are a steady stream of people that keep the lowest price of a particular GPU core at a steady state, with fluctuations according to this week's supply.

So I think that GN's data is correct, but that their interpretation of the data is wrong. They are in the Correlation vs Causation area of wrong data analysis. The reason why video cards are selling so close to the MSRP of the next card up is correlation, not causation. The real reason why cards are selling at their current prices is because all cards are priced based off of the 3090's scalped price. Not the 3090's MSRP, but what people are willing to pay for the 3090's performance. No one is going to pay scalped 3090 prices for a 3080 Ti when they can get the "better" card for the same price. And as long as people are paying $2,700+ for the 3090, then the 3080 Ti will always sell for less than that, and thus begins the chain reaction.

comments.text:
@Ozpin So I'm a scalper, I've sold 4 dozen GPUs in the last 3 months and have over $50,000 in revenue and I am constantly monitoring the fluctuations in prices. I also talk to other scalpers and I am a part of a few scalping groups. 

What I will say about GN's interpretation is that it can be applied to certain AIB partner cards that are AMD based. What us scalpers are seeing is that many AIB partners are pricing their AMD cards very close to what their performance level gets you if you were to buy a scalped card. This makes buying those cards for scalping not very feasible because of platform fees on places like eBay and Facebook Marketplace. You have to have a good amount of local face-to-face sales to make scalping those cards profitable. This also applies to a few 3090 and 3080 Ti models (I'm looking at you, Zotac AMP HOLOs) This makes it much easier to get one of those cards from an online retailer instead of a scalper. So high MSRPs definitely affects what people are actually paying, since even those high MSRP cards sell out very quickly. But it is a slightly different context than what the debate has turned into.

My take on the pricing in the scalped market is that it is primarily based off of how much the market is willing to pay for the highest performing card, which is the 3090. What people are willing to pay for a 3090 is what dictates what people are willing to pay for a 3080, 3070, 6900 XT, etc. This also applies to previous generation cards.. the performance of a 2080 Ti compared to the 3070 and 3080 absolutely dictates it's price in the 3rd party market. All of the previous generation cards are currently selling at prices compared to the latest generation's performance. We also see this phenomenon with EVGA's B-Stock and Zotac's refurbished cards that they both sell 1st party on their website. They are able to charge the highest MSRP that those refurbished cards were sold at when they were new because people are snatching them up as a "great deal" because a used 2080 Super still has a ton of performance. In normal market conditions those refurbished cards would NOT be selling for full New MSRP. I have bought many of these 1st party refurbished cards and so this isn't 2nd hand knowledge.

Also, what we've seen when a new card comes on the market, is that higher performing cards get a price increase in 3rd party sales, and lower performing cards have a slight decrease in price but do not experience as much change as the higher performing cards.

To give an overview of the scalping market, what we scalpers do is provide a scatter plot of prices and the buyers decide what they're willing to pay. Some buyers just want the lowest Buy it Now price and don't care about the specific card, just the specific GPU and sometimes not even then as they just want the best GPU for what their budget allows, and those buyers set the floor for pricing. Anything under this price gets bought by people with ebay search alerts because they want a video card at a lower price than what they can immediately buy it for. It is the buyers who don't wait for a particular price and just want a GPU right now that fits their budget that really dictate the price of all cards. Other buyers want a specific GPU (Color, factory overclock, pre-installed waterblock, etc.) And buy the lowest price of that even if it is hundreds of dollars more than the lowest priced version of that GPU core. Others want a specific GPU but want to wait until someone posts it for the lowest price that GPU core sells for and so they have ebay alerts and buy as soon as what they want is at a price they want. 

But again we come back to the people who are ready to buy right now and they will buy the best performance that their budget allows for. If their budget is $1,000 for a video card, they are going to buy a 3060 or 6700 XT because that's the highest performance that they can click a Buy it Now button on. And these people represent the majority of buyers. And those buyers come from different situations. Maybe their old video card died. Maybe they are finally done waiting for reasonable prices and just want to game right now. Maybe they are a business that has a customer who needs a new computer. Whoever they are, they are in my stated category of people wanting the best performance for Buy it Now and they are a steady stream of people that keep the lowest price of a particular GPU core at a steady state, with fluctuations according to this week's supply.

So I think that GN's data is correct, but that their interpretation of the data is wrong. They are in the Correlation vs Causation area of wrong data analysis. The reason why video cards are selling so close to the MSRP of the next card up is correlation, not causation. The real reason why cards are selling at their current prices is because all cards are priced based off of the 3090's scalped price. Not the 3090's MSRP, but what people are willing to pay for the 3090's performance. No one is going to pay scalped 3090 prices for a 3080 Ti when they can get the "better" card for the same price. And as long as people are paying $2,700+ for the 3090, then the 3080 Ti will always sell for less than that, and thus begins the chain reaction.

comments.text:
You missed the point. 

Let's say that MSRP is set at $1,000,000 for the 3070Ti. Do you think they will sell on eBay for >$1m? 

No. Of course they won't. Not because scalpers wouldn't be willing to but because no one will buy. 

MSRP doesn't effect how much someone is willing to pay for something (well, there's some psychological components, but let's not be pedantic)... in a situation where demand far outstrips supply, the costs rise until demand drops below supply. If people are willing to pay $2000 for a 3080 today, they aren't going to pay $1m tomorrow just because MSRP changed. 

So MSRP does not change prices... it changes profitability. Price is set by scarcity combined with perceived value. 

Raising the MSRP might stop scalping (good), or might reduce scalpers profits and instead put it in the hands of the company that makes the product (good); but it won't raise what the market is willing to pay for the product.

Similar to Linus, I defended the RTX 3080 Ti as a good choice for enthusiast gamers with big budgets who want the performance of an RTX 3090 at a lower price.
The RTX 3070 Ti is indefensible. It's worse value than the RTX 3080 and barely faster than the RTX 3070. 8GB is likely to be a major limitation for a card that fast in next gen games, and the RTX 3070 was never particularly good value to begin with, even at MSRP - the 3060 Ti is nearly as fast and has the same amount of VRAM for a significantly lower price.
Linus isn't really wrong in saying that it makes sense to buy the RTX 3070 Ti if you find it at MSRP, considering the state of the current market, but I'd argue that it makes far more sense to wait for a GPU that's actually good to become available at MSRP. I still agree with part of his 3080ti review where he mentions that two 3080ti cards can be made from the parts of one 3090, but this really rides on the back of Nvidia putting a pause on 3090 production to validate his claim, which currently there is no official statement. Still, it at least gives some credence to the 3080ti's existence, even if I still think the price is too high. Then again it could be that this is the first of the MSRP price hike we're seeing as a result of all of this shortage nonsense going on. I'll be curious what prices future AMD cards have, when they come around.

The 3070ti though? I don't know why it exists. This feels like the Super series from last generation, except now we don't live in a market where there's enough surplus to shrug it off if it's uninteresting. Instead we know that it's diluting an already exhausted market. This is where AMD has a chance to shine, where they continue sticking it out with their current lineup and wait for their next generation GPUs to really make up for the few very small shortcomings they have from Nvidia products, and then advertise the new cards as straight upgrades instead of questionable product fluff. And hopefully there's less of a shortage issue by then.

comments.text:
NVIDIA buys wafers. The supply is in terms of wafers. Binning doesn't "dilute supply". Coming out with a SKU that is a higher binned part of an already existing SKU does not effect the total supply, it just makes more (computationally, economically) efficient use of the supply that is available. there are still 100 GPUs available no matter if those 100 GPUs consist of 100 3070s or 70 3070s and 30 3070Tis.

The product is not meant to "help the situation" any more than it's meant to "bring about world peace". It just targets end user markets in whatever the situation happens to be. It's good for NVIDIA and it's good for the people who are looking for a card faster than the 3070 but slower than the 3080. Yes, if NVIDIA decided to give away free performance by down-SKUing dies that could reach better performance then there would be a larger volume of cards available to people who want 3070 performance but not 3070 Ti performance. But in actuality that would mean lower margins for NVIDIA and would apply pressure on NVIDIA to raise prices on all 3070s to compensate.

Stop being an entitled whiner and instead learn some economics.

comments.text:
As someone who has sold/resold many GPUs over the years, including new-in-box gpus and full systems, and does gaming and mining on a used system: Linus is almost definitely right here, and you're way, way off. It's also unfair to say the red bars vastly overshooting the blue bars undermines his point, since that's also part of his point, and is at worst neutral towards his position. It really only undermines yours: that MSRP is of any kind of particular importance for resale value. The correlation you did find seems to be simply that more expensive cards at launch are typically more expensive later as well, which would be expected because they're also typically more powerful and useful. For MSRP to have some kind of significant effect they'd have to be much more tightly clustered, and with many fewer counterexamples. 

The concerns of people who are buying cards second hand aren't 1:1 with unbounded performance per dollar either, for a few reasons:
• Total system cost is a factor. If you're paying $500 for the rest of your system, paying $400 instead of $300 for a GPU that's only 15% faster actually sounds fine. The used market in particular is much more GPU-limited because of the lower fps targets (30-60fps minimums in almost anything 2+ years old can be achieved with nearly any CPU) and the glut of cheap high core count cpus.
• Used buyers are typically targeting performance in just a few specific games like CS:GO + Apex Legends or Fortnite + Minecraft.
• Second hand buyers in general care about resale value and depreciation. Some cards depreciate faster than others for reasons such as: 
• VRAM: Higher VRAM for older gpus is extremely important. Performance wise a 580 8GB and 4GB aren't much different, except in cases where VRAM is maxxed out in which case 580 tanks. 580 8GB in my experience has typically commanded a 1.5-2x price as a result. This is particularly true for 980ti vs 980, 1080ti vs 1080, and Nvidia vs AMD comparisons as well. This effect is amplified by the next point: 
• Mining performance is often unrelated to gaming performance, for example Vega 56 during mining booms are much more expensive than even 1080s, but often are found cheaper outside of them. 980ti (6GB) is up to a ridiculous 3x as profitable for long stretches (months or more) as a 980 (4GB) despite being relatively close in gaming performance and VRAM. 1080ti can be over 50% more profitable for long term mining than a 1080 similarly. The best example of this is the Radeon VII (16GB) which costs multiple thousands of dollars during mining booms, and even today costs a ridiculous 2-3x an RTX 3070 despite a $700 launch price and a common $500 sale price at retailers and second hand.






















Still prefer you to Linus though.

While I largely agree with Steve's point, I think it's simply a difference in perspective. 

Steve thinks (rightfully) that the 3090 is super overkill for gaming and costs too much for the performance and therefore is a workstation card and not a gaming card. Therefore a 3080 Ti should be compared to a 3080 gaming wise and not a 3090.

Linus does the opposite, he essentially thinks that while the 3090 is overkill, it IS still the best for gaming and focuses on gaming performance. Therefore the 3080 ti is one step down from the 3090, instead of one step above the 3080, and should be compared to the 3080 Ti. 

In which case Linus makes sense, if you want 3090 gaming performance, then the 3080 Ti is a great deal because it costs 300 dollars less than the 3090. If you don't think the 3090 counts as a gaming card and therefore only compare the 3080 vs 3080 Ti, then the 3080 Ti is a HORRIBLE deal. It's all perspective.

comments.text: Your comparison methodology doesn't make sense for the thing you're trying to get at. You want MSRP influence vs performance influence; merely looking at relative MSRPs cannot, even in theory, demonstrate that. You also cannot compare mere relative performance, because gaming is largely a step function: can this card hit 60fps (or 120fps, or 240fps, or whatever) at the resolution I want to run it at? (I know from experience I bought a used 1080Ti because it could hit or come close to playable framerates on a 4k monitor, while the 1080 couldn't.) A moderate increase in performance could, therefore, represent a significant improvement in value, if it happens to cross one of the step-function thresholds. Trying to account for that would be a huge amount of work, of course, but bad data is not better than no data.

I think the main argument for anybody with a currently good GPU in their system shopping the 30-series is the market is messed up for their current GPU as well. I bought a 2070 non-super near launch for around $450 after rebates and now they're selling used for $700+ which is kind of crazy. That just self-funds an upgrade whereas if the market normalizes it really shouldn't be selling for more than $300-350. This isn't a knock against your review or your analysis here--like you said, you can't account for everybody's personal situation and when it comes to how you should spend the money your analysis still holds--but just an observation for why I think people with cards are jumping on this stuff as well. In your opening gas analogy, it's like if a large portion of the panic buying market also has gas to sell.

If the choice is between an effectively $0 upgrade right now--or an upgrade with cash in the pocket--versus a nebulous value upgrade in the future? It sucks, but I think that's the decision some people are making if they can actually find these cards at MSRP. Effectively, you can personally make more money selling an older Nvidia product than Nvidia made on selling it to you. Nvidia is then selling you products for more than they really should be, but on net you are still coming out better. That's just insane.

comments.text:
So will you guys start to sell some premium ground beef in the store, to capitalize on the disagreement (the scandal!) with Linus? On a serious note - Linus doesn't really seem to be a bad guy. But some of his stances on hardware and technological industry at large are... weird. Not even because I disagree with them, it's just weird. Say, his "tied to real world performance and what is available on the market" - that's the thing though. There isn't anything available on the market. He himself created an entire project dedicated to putting GPUs into gamer hands (good on him, praiseworthy) specifically because of that. In a market where demand vastly outpaces the production/availability - normal market methodology for price forming doesn't apply. It is an abnormal state of the market. That's why there are generally a lot of regulations placed around market, cause it actually doesn't really behave that well when the boat is rocked hard.

Not to be a stinker, but your price graphs might corroborate your point of view, not prove it. Correlation doesn't equal causation unless the link is established beyond reasonable doubt. As I'm sure you are aware. I fully agree with your point of view in general. It is insanity to assume that MSRP doesn't affect (in a major way) the market pricing for the product. For 3rd party manufacturers, for scalpers, for consumers. It sets an expectation of what is "acceptable pricing" of the product, directly and indirectly. If anything, in current conditions perceived value is even further inflated due to limited stock of the product. Not deflated due to small difference in performance (as Linus seemed to imply, if I understood him). That said, proving this connection beyond reasonable doubt would be a monumental task. You're operating in the market governed by human interaction (which is often hard to predict and illogical), in the state of the market that can be described as many things but normal. I guess I just wanted to say "let's be very careful with statements when presenting such graphs". It exposes your side to some very nasty basic counterarguments.

Let's go very basic. If in a desert, thousands are dying of thirst and there is a salesman offering a hundred cups of water - people would just buy it at a proposed price. They would pay even more if they're asked. Because the difference here isn't "I don't like the price, I'll go elsewhere to buy this product". The difference here is "I don't like this price... I won't buy this product any time soon". Yes, there is AMD, and they seem to be less eager to scalp their customers. But they're still suffering from same abnormal conditions on the market that inflate the pricing and prevent them from properly competing against scalpers. In a properly working market - scalpers can't thrive, their presence is a very big indication of an abnormal state of the market. Since scalping requires monopolization, either singlehanded or collective, of the stock. GPUs aren't as essential as water? Why, yes, perfectly reasonable pointing out of the flaw of my argument. But for some hardware can be very much important and not just a luxury. It may be required for work, for example, and previous computer is just non-functional. They can't wait for a new one. They HAVE to participate in current market, HAVE to get the product no matter the price. While not necessarily linked to high end GPUs in general, COVID-19 sparked such situation with a lot of households upgrading/replacing their computers. Again, scalpers are an indication of the abnormal and illogical state of the market.

Maybe NVidia wants more money. Surely they do. All companies do. But joining in with the effort of scalping is merely them putting more money in their pocket at the expense of the end buyers - us, consumers. Scalpers won't get hit by that, they'll just mark up the GPU even more. What can hit them is the resolution of the disparity between demand and stock on offer. Which isn't in sight yet. One can pretend NVidia's decision won't affect end users. I'm sure NVidia is very much going to in their PR. Doesn't change the reality. In a system with finite money, for someone to profit more - someone must pay more.

Seems like he used to be one of the better channels for commonly useful topics in this field years ago, and he's still popular largely off that early success even though there are better channels now.

In particular one of the things that really turned me off to him, was the old experiment they did, stuffing a PC case with small objects, then more, then suffocating it completely with crap, and showing little difference in thermal performance to prove that putting a figurine or whatever in your case doesn't affect airflow.

The methodology for that was so terrible that they didn't even show the system configuration. Like we never got to see how the fans were setup. Because it looked to me like it didn't actually have good airflow to begin with, which could explain why the control was not much better than the experiment. We also didn't see how stressed the components were. Were they stressed enough to thermal throttle in the first place? Well we don't know, they didn't show us.

Imagine kind of telling us what your experiment was, yet not even including critical information about it, and then using that to reach a conclusion which none of us can argue with because you didn't actually show or tell us what you did. People are still pushing that video today, despite the fact that you can easily try this at home using your own PC, with a good mesh case and reasonable fan config, and see very different results than Linus got.

Like FFS, if people like Steve at GN or any other channel like AVTechy who review cases can show measurable temp drops just from a slightly more efficient case design, then sure as hell stuffing the case with clothes until there's zero space left in it, is going to affect thermals.

comments.text:
I think both are right in a sense and are kinda talking past the other. 

Linus's point is that everyone is going to want to buy these cards at MSRP because the innate value is much higher based upon the market. He also states that the 3080ti slots into a spot that is below the 3090 and not so much an uplift of the 3080 which allows NVidia to produce more chips than they would with 3090s because of the difference in RAM. That framing makes a world of difference. His points about the second hand market value is more in terms of normal supply and demand and not the topsy turvey world that we live in whereas Steve highlighted today's current market (Linus did mention that these are not normal times in the Wan Show). 

Steve is pressing on the point that with the current state of the market NVidia releasing another line of cards you cannot buy for a marginal performance gain is a slap in the face to gamers. I completely get it, another card no one will be able to buy leads to feel bads all over the place. My problem with the take is just that these chips were likely in the works to be released early this year and were derailed as a result of the worldwide supply issues. Jayz2Cents made the point that NVidia does not want this situation as much as anyone else. They would much prefer that everyone be able to buy a GPU, but at the same time they cannot stop their progress on new products even though the current world will not receive it with open arms as they would in normal times.

I love both channels and tune into both daily. Steve is channeling more anger at the situation than Linus is and he is not wrong to do so, but at the end of the day, the salt doesn't really help that much. This time sucks for everyone and it hurts not just these guys, but the community as a whole. Just hold strong everyone, this will end sooner or later. Don't give into scalpers if you can help it.

comments.text: The 3080 Ti exists to eliminate the 3080 from the product stack, because Nvidia wants to make more money. The 3080 is made from the same GP102 die from which the 3090 is also made. Essentially, the 3080 is going to become even more of a unicorn. This is Nvidia's real play, and Linus missed it.
